findings.source_passage: but man, in the ideal, is so noble and so sparkling, such a grand and glowing creature, that over any ignominious blemish in him all his fellows should run to throw their costliest robes.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'But were the coming narrative'
findings.why_it_matters: This is one of the most critically cited passages in the chapter, establishing Melville's democratic-humanist thesis. Its rhetorical grandeur and specific phrasing ('noble and so sparkling,' 'grand and glowing creature,' 'costliest robes') are signature prose; losing it collapses the philosophical architecture of the chapter.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the core sentence verbatim or near-verbatim: 'but man, in the ideal, is so noble and so sparkling, such a grand and glowing creature, that over any ignominious blemish in him all his fellows should run to throw their costliest robes.'

findings.source_passage: thou great democratic God! who didst not refuse to the swart convict, Bunyan, the pale, poetic pearl; Thou who didst clothe with doubly hammered leaves of finest gold, the stumped and paupered arm of old Cervantes; Thou who didst pick up Andrew Jackson from the pebbles; who didst hurl him upon a war-horse; who didst thunder him higher than a throne!
findings.why_it_matters: The Bunyan/Cervantes/Andrew Jackson invocation is one of the most famous and critically discussed passages in all of Moby-Dick; it grounds Melville's democratic aesthetics in concrete historical figures and is cited in virtually every critical treatment of the novel's politics and ambition.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the invocation of Bunyan, Cervantes, and Jackson verbatim or in near-verbatim compression; this material cannot be dropped without catastrophic signature loss.

findings.source_passage: That immaculate manliness we feel within ourselves, so far within us, that it remains intact though all the outer character seem gone; bleeds with keenest anguish at the undraped spectacle of a valor-ruined man.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'But were the coming narrative'
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence is rhetorically and thematically distinctive—'immaculate manliness,' 'undraped spectacle of a valor-ruined man'—and carries critical weight regarding Starbuck's eventual fate and Melville's moral vision. Its erasure removes the interpretive fulcrum of the chapter.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the 'immaculate manliness' sentence and the 'valor-ruined man' formulation, even in a compressed form that preserves the key phrases.

findings.source_passage: Thou shalt see it shining in the arm that wields a pick or drives a spike; that democratic dignity which, on all hands, radiates without end from God; Himself! The great God absolute! The centre and circumference of all democracy! His omnipresence, our divine equality!
findings.why_it_matters: The exclamatory climax—'The great God absolute! The centre and circumference of all democracy!'—is one of Melville's most famous rhetorical peaks and a locus of critical attention on his democratic theology. The draft reduces this to a flat paraphrase ('radiates from God Himself') stripping the ecstatic register entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the exclamatory sequence verbatim: 'The great God absolute! The centre and circumference of all democracy! His omnipresence, our divine equality!'

findings.source_passage: But we shall ere long see what that word 'careful' precisely means when used by a man like Stubb, or almost any other whale hunter.
findings.why_it_matters: Stubb's brief appearance and the narrator's ironic aside about the meaning of 'careful' is a voice-establishing moment of Melvillean dramatic irony that foreshadows the novel's action; its omission erases both the irony and the introduction of Stubb.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Stubb's line and the narrator's ironic gloss in a single compressed sentence.

findings.source_passage: Nor can piety itself, at such a shameful sight, completely stifle her upbraidings against the permitting stars.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'But were the coming narrative'
findings.why_it_matters: This phrase foreshadows the theological tension surrounding Starbuck's failure to act against Ahab and registers the narrator's critique of divine permissiveness—a thematically load-bearing sentence for critics reading Starbuck's arc.
findings.suggested_fix: Include the 'permitting stars' clause when restoring the valor-ruined man passage.

summary: The draft catastrophically drops the Bunyan/Cervantes/Jackson invocation, the 'immaculate manliness'/'valor-ruined man' passage, the 'great God absolute' exclamatory climax, and Stubb's ironic cameo—losing the four most critically famous passages in the chapter and gutting the democratic-theological argument that is the chapter's entire second half.
